Harnessing nature for next‑generation ­CO2 removal

Hegang Zhi, Department of Mechanical Engineering, University of Michigan, Ann Arbor, MI 48109, USA Songtao  Yang, and Jiushi  Ma, Department of  Mechanical Engineering, University of  Michigan, Ann  Arbor, MI  48109, USA; Macromolecular Science and Engineering, University of Michigan, Ann Arbor, MI 48109, USA Julian Ignacio Lopez, and Jing Tang  , Department of Mechanical Engineering, University of Michigan, Ann Arbor, MI 48109, USA

Address all correspondence to Jing Tang at jingtang@umich.edu

(Received 15 April 2025; accepted 27 May 2025; published online: 13 June 2025)

Abstract Achieving carbon neutrality necessitates a variety of strategies, including the adoption of renewable energy with zero carbon emissions, utilization of low-carbon fuels, and significant reduction in anthropogenic emissions, with a strong emphasis on carbon dioxide ­(CO2) capture technologies. These technologies are essential for significantly lowering atmospheric ­CO2 levels. Current methods of carbon capture, such as the use of metalorganic frameworks, amine solvents, and ionic liquids, excel in high surface areas, porosity, and reactive functional groups. However, they involve sophistication and costly production processes. This review proposes a shift toward materials engineered from naturally derived compounds and bioinspired mechanisms, enhancing the accessibility and sustainability of ­CO2 sorption. This prospective aims to explore and bridge advancements in naturally derived or inspired ­CO2 capture materials and methods, assessing their physical and chemical structures, sorption mechanisms, and capabilities. This article will compare these nature-inspired materials to contemporary artificial technologies, highlighting their potential for the next generation of adsorbent and absorbent materials, including solid, liquid, and mixed-state, characterized by rapid kinetics, high efficiency, sustainability, and stability in ­CO2 sorption.

Introduction The accelerating need to mitigate greenhouse effects in the atmosphere has driven the development of material science and engineering to reduce greenhouse gas emissions by capturing, utilizing, and sequestering ­CO2.[1,2] The scaling-up of the material for carbon removal has been limited by the operational cost of the material for ­CO2 capture directly and indirectly from the air, ascribed to their chemical usage, metal incorporation, and energy input for manufacturing.[3–5]

Historically, efforts to mitigate ­CO2 emissions have predominantly relied on traditional carbon capture methods, notably physical and chemical absorption and adsorption.[6] A widely adopted conventional technique involves aqueous amine solutions, such as monoethanolamine (MEA), diethanolamine (DEA), and methyl diethanolamine (MDEA), which chemically absorb ­CO2 through reversible acid-base reactions.[7–9] In these systems, ­CO2 reacts with amines to form carbonates and bicarbonates, capturing approximately 2–6 mol ­CO2 ­L−1 solvent.[8,10,11] While their efficiency can be improved by mixing the diverse amine solvents, these processes are energetically demanding due to the continuous high temperature required for regeneration (1107–2211 kJ ­mol−1 ­CO2), involve significant solvent degradation over cycles, and chemical consumption issues that elevate both economic and environmental costs.[8]

Solid adsorbent-based technologies represent another conventional strategy, where synthetic materials such as activated carbon, zeolites, silica gels, and metal-organic frameworks (MOFs) have been developed with enlarged surfaces and pore structures for enhanced ­CO2 adsorption capacity.[12–15] Owing to the inherent physisorption of gas, these solid-state materials can also be enhanced by chemisorption mechanisms driven by various carbon bonds with functional groups, allowing moderate ­CO2 uptake capacities ranging between 1.2 and 9  mmol ­g−1 at room temperature and pressure.[5] While providing elevated ­CO2 sorption rate compared to amine solutions, these adsorbents confront challenges including limited selectivity for ­CO2 over other gases, reduced capacity under humid conditions, and intricate synthesis methods for cost over $500 ­kg−1.[16] Despite their tunable properties and high adsorption capacities, MOFs require sophisticated synthetic routes and costly precursor chemicals, which limit their scalability and practical application. Given the inherent limitations of conventional carbon capture methodologies, attention has increasingly shifted toward leveraging nature as an inspiration or derivation. Nature-based materials exhibit adsorption capacities in the range of approximately 0.9–7 mmol ­g−1 at room temperature and pressure, comparable to synthetic adsorbents, yet with significantly reduced economic and environmental costs.[17] Materials directly derived from natural resources, such as lignin, cellulose, and chitosan, demonstrate significant potential Hegang Zhi and Songtao Yang have contributed equally to this work.

due to their accessibility, renewability, facile modifications, low environmental impact, and comparable ­CO2 capture capacities. For instance, deriving from wood pulp and paper industry as byproduct, kraft lignin, is globally available at an extractable volume of 25–40 million tons per year and can be isolated using commercial acid precipitation processes at costs as low as $16–40 per ton, making it an economically attractive and scalable feedstock for ­CO2 capture materials.[18] Nature also efficiently fluxes carbon through processes such as photosynthesis, mineralization, and photocatalysis, inspiring innovative technologies that offer sustainable and economically viable alternatives for carbon capture. Moreover, materials directly derived from nature, hybridized with natural-inspired mechanistic methods, provide pathways to overcome existing material performance barriers through biomimicry and structural optimization. This review systematically emphasizes the recent advancements and potential of ­CO2 removal materials and pathways by harnessing the intrinsic values from nature, categorized into directly derived, indirectly inspired, and hybrid routes. It assesses the underlying principles, mechanisms, and comparative effectiveness of these emerging technologies against traditional methods. Additionally, this work summarizes current challenges, including trade-offs

between capture efficiency, cost, and environmental footprint, and outlines future opportunities in material innovation and process optimization.

Materials derived from nature In nature, numerous materials have abundant reserves and unique structures that show prospects for chemical modification for ­CO2 capture.[19] Among these, plant-based polymers such as cellulose, lignin, and starch are of great interest due to their wide availability, offering accessible reactive sites for chemical reactions, such as hydroxyl and amine, and exhibiting favorable morphology that can advance material design. As depicted in Fig. 1, two of the most widely accepted chemical modification methods are alkaline attachment and amine addition, and the additional capture sites facilitate ­CO2 sorption mechanisms and kinetics. Moreover, the biodegradability of plant-based chemicals makes them an eco-friendly choice for ­CO2 capture. Cellulose and lignin are primarily derived from biomass such as wood and crops.[20] In wood, these two polymers, along with hemicellulose, form chemical crosslinks that make it challenging to extract exclusive cellulose, lignin, or glucose ­monomers[21] [Fig. 2(a)]. There are multiple ways for separating these chemicals from each other, including hydrolysis,

Serving as a plant’s energy storage, starch is usually found in the form of macron-scale particles rather than as polymer chains or crystalline structures like cellulose. This simplicity means that starch can be more conveniently extracted from plants through various methods.[25]

In terms of carbon capture, these three materials are explored because they are abundant in many adjustable chemical groups and reactive sites that can be modified for high-efficiency ­CO2 capture. One common approach focuses on modifying the polymeric structure through the substitution or addition of amine groups to enhance ­CO2 selectivity. Ho et al. concluded that modifying cellulose-based materials could create membranes with improved selectivity for carbon capture.[20] This strategy underscores the importance of chemical tailoring in achieving efficient ­CO2 separation. In another similar work, Guillermo’s group explored the use of alkali-dissolved cellulose.[26] By dissolving cellulose under alkaline conditions, they were able to effectively capture and sequester ­CO2, demonstrating another leading pathway in carbon capture. With a different precursor material, Sreedhar’s work introduced starch-based porous carbon materials.[25] Through several steps of drying and pyrolysis, these materials are ultimately designed for high-capacity amine loading, which not only increases the available reactive sites but also improves

overall ­CO2 capture performance, up to 3.4 mmol ­g−1. This approach highlights the role of porosity in accommodating more amine groups for effective gas adsorption, supporting the importance of the physical morphology during adsorbent design. Another innovative route involves the use of transition metal coordination in naturally derived materials. Beyond cellulose and starch, biopolymers, such as lignin, also offer promising pathways. For instance, Ghorai and colleagues investigated the ­CO2 capture mechanism of ionized lignin.[27] This work broadens the scope by demonstrating that biomass lignin, when ionized to expose hydroxide reactive sites, can contribute to effective carbon capture, showcasing the versatility of bio-based materials. Furthermore, structural cellulose and lignin materials can even be specially optimized into advanced structural adsorbents, such as the synthesis of cellulosic aerogel in the research by Zhang et al.[28] These aerogels demonstrated excellent gas permeability, high surface area, and even electrical conductivity properties that not only support efficient ­CO2 capture but also pave the way for multifunctional applications. In addition to the above-mentioned natural-inspired materials with abundant reserves in nature, chitin and chitosan are also common materials of biological sources with extremely high natural abundance [Fig. 2(b)]. These two substances mainly assist in forming the shells of Crustaceans and are also the structural components of fungal organisms, which is one of the abundant polysaccharides in nature, with the chemical composition of its polymer monomer being N-acetylglucosamine.[29] The abundant amine and hydroxyl groups exposed can empower it with a distinctive solubility

and stronger reactivity with certain modifications. Their adsorption capacity can be enhanced due to the improvement from acid-base reaction and H-bonding on the adsorbents.[30] The morphology and composition of chitosan and chitin vary with molecular length and often feature highly crystalline or parallel pellet structures. Physical and chemical extraction methods enable the derivation of adsorbent material from chitosan/chitin, while the latter is preferred for ameliorated solubility and a wide range of derivatives.[31] Specifically, naturally acquired chitosan/chitin is accompanied by carbonates and proteins, which require steps such as carbonation and alkaline deproteinization, before the modification toward ­CO2 adsorbents.[32] In direct carbonation, chitosan is subjected to high temperatures (between 600 and 800℃) to produce nitrogen-doped porous carbon, which significantly increases the material’s surface area and pore volume, thus elevating its available sites for gas adsorption.[30] On the other hand, chemical activation is carried out by incorporating strong bases such as KOH or NaOH during the carbonization process, leading to an enlarged pore distribution, e.g., micropores and mesopores, and retaining the nitrogen functionalities that contribute to active binding sites for chemisorption.[33] Besides, the hybrid strategies are also investigated by combining chitosan with other functional materials, such as carbonbased materials, zeolites, or ionic liquids to leverage both the functional groups of chitosan and the porous structures provided by the additional components, leading synergistic effects such as persistent adsorption-desorption cyclability, lower operating expenses and reduced carbon footprints, maintaining superior ­CO2 capture performance.[34–36] During carbon capture processes, the various modification approaches promote the reaction of functional groups with ­CO2 in fast kinetics to form bicarbonate or carbamate species, enhancing the selectivity and adsorption capacity to ~ 8 mmol ­g−1 at maximum.[30]

Biochar materials are carbonaceous material directly derived from the pyrolysis of variety of plant-based biomass feedstocks, with their primary constituent being porous dehydrated carbon.[37] At lower pyrolysis temperatures (< 400℃), biochar predominantly comprises amorphous carbon; in contrast, when subjected to higher temperatures (~ 600℃), the pyrolysis process tends to yield biochar that is largely composed of aromatics and hydrocarbons.[38] Owing to its high carbon concentration and inherent thermal stability, biochar offers significant advantages for ­CO2 sequestration; it maintains fixed carbon without significant environmental impacts.[39] Additionally, innovative modification strategies for biochar have been developed to boost its performance in capturing ­CO2, and several distinct approaches illustrate its versatility.[40] One method uses alkaline treatment with agents like KOH or NaOH to etch the carbon matrix, thereby expanding the pore structure and creating additional adsorption sites through increased microporosity.[41] A further common approach involves the grafting of amine groups onto the biochar surface, a process that enhances chemical interactions with ­CO2 by introducing

nitrogen-containing functionalities that improve affinity.[17] Concerning the economic viability biochar as a naturally derived ­CO2 adsorbent, studies showing that physical and chemical activation processing various biomass residues can achieve production costs down to $1.5 and 3 per kg, while switching to renewable energy for pyrolysis further reduces the processing cost of biochar to $1.04 per kg, both outperforming commercial activated carbon regarding cost advantages and greenhouse warming potential.[37,42] Together, these tailored modification techniques highlight the adaptability of biochar and promise it as a cost-effective, sustainable candidate for advanced carbon capture applications. Geologic materials are naturally developed materials from the underground. Many underground materials, such as soils, clays, stones, and minerals, are slightly alkaline, making them naturally suitable for large-scale carbon capture. Among these, research has focused on materials like basalt, olivine, and serpentine for engineered ­CO2 mineralization due to their high cation content and basic conditions.[43] The silicate in the rock could degrade into silicic acid and cations, both of which could support carbon capture kinetically, and the material itself is very cost-effective. The large storage amount of silicates underground is very promising for the development of a low-cost carbon capture adsorbent. As a geologically formed material, clay is a diverse, naturally abundant soil material primarily serving as an amorphous solid adsorbent for carbon dioxide capture through rock weathering and hydrolysis processes, such as principal varieties include kaolinite, montmorillonite, smectite, and ­gibbsite[44] [Fig. 2(c)]. Due to its amorphous nature, clay-based materials can consume less energy during ­CO2 capture reactions, while their high natural abundance enhances the overall economic feasibility of the process.[45] The modification and optimization of clay materials focus on raising the alkaline component percentage and amine attachment. Chen et al. utilized kaolinite as a kind of carbon capture adsorbent and finally sequestrated clay and carbonate in a new type of cement substitute, while the scalability was limited by the cost of chemical modifications.[46] Research focused on underground carbon sequestration directly within the kaolinite layer, particularly in the presence of water.[47] The chemical enhancement of the cation level is investigated, due to they are effective capturing agents for carbon capture.

Materials inspired by nature CO2 concentrating through photosynthesis is also a common carbon capture technique. Photosynthetic microorganisms, including cyanobacteria, can adapt and grow at various ambient ­CO2 concentrations due to the unique Carbon Concentrating Mechanism (CCM).[48] CCM [Fig. 3(b)] can overcome the defects of RuBisCO (ribulose-1,5-bisphosphate carboxylase/ oxygenase), including its slow catalytic rate and its easy binding with oxygen.[49] At the same time, it can elevate the inner ­CO2 concentration of cells and inhibit photorespiration when experiencing a low ­CO2 environment. Carboxysomes are microcellular compartments (~ 100–400 nm in diameter) in cyanobacterial cells encapsulated by a protein shell and enriched internally with RuBisCO and CA, and ­HCO3 − enters the carboxysomes by diffusion or active transport and is converted to ­CO2 catalyzed by CA. Due to the restriction of gas diffusion by the protein shell of the carboxysomes, ­CO2 is confined, and the concentration rises sharply as a result of the conversion and storage of ­CO2 biologically. Additionally, ­CO2 can be converted into carbohydrates in bacterial activities. Through cyanobacterial photosynthesis, ­CO2 can be directly and stably converted into glucose, elucidating the pathways and mutations leading to glucose synthesis and secretion.[50] With optimized glucose synthesis properties of recombinant strains, the strain secreted more than 5 g ­L−1 of glucose, accounting for 70% of the fixed carbon source. Recent work also demonstrates faster bioethanol production via flue gases by modifying cyanobacteria [Fig. 3(a)].[51] By introducing the groESL gene and co-expressing it with ictB and ecaA, it can be used to sequester ­CO2 from flue gas for ethanol production in large quantities from ­CO2 collected by CCM in cyanobacteria. With a regulation of cyanobacteria genes, and an accelerated rate of sycrose production up to 1.9 g ­L−1 ­day−1 is revealed due to the activation of the sucrose biosynthesis pathway under salt stress conditions [Fig. 3(c and d)].[52]

Similarly, in plants and algae, photosynthesis occurs in a specialized intracellular organelle, the chloroplast, which

also inspires the carbon capture methodology [Fig. 3(e)].[53] The process of carbon capture in chloroplasts is known as the Calvin cycle and is divided into three stages: carboxylation, reduction reaction, and regeneration of ribulose-1,5- bisphosphate (RuBP). ­CO2 entering chloroplasts by free diffusion can catalytically generate unstable six-carbon intermediates with RuBP and rapidly decompose into two 3-phosphoglyceric acids (PGA). ATP and NADPH rapidly convert 3-PGA to Glyceraldehyde-3-Phosphate (G3P), which is used for the regeneration of RuBP and the synthesis of saccharides. Current research focuses on improving carbon capture efficiency and producing desired products by genetically engineering modified RuBisCO activity, optimizing photorespiration, or mimicking chloroplast mechanisms (e.g., artificial photosynthetic systems). Nogalska et al. demonstrated an artificial photosynthesis system inspired by the process of carbon dioxide absorption from the atmosphere by leaves.[54] A designed porous polysulfide membrane contactor, mimicking the process of ­CO2 entry into the cell, successfully converts the captured carbon into methanol or other hydrocarbons. The system achieves assimilation rates ranging from 6 to 160 μmol ­m−2 ­s−1, which is in the same range as the rate of natural leaves, demonstrating that the captured ­CO2 can be further used for the synthesis of desired carbon products. Tu et al. developed a carbon capture process of photosynthesis based on rhodopsin, where the gene was engineered to utilize the proton motive force generated by light-activated retinal plasma to power ATP and NADPH synthesis.[55] Overexpression of β-carbonic anhydrase (CAN) enhanced ­CO2 fixation as increased CAN

In addition to genetic modifications of cyanobacteria, algaederived bio-oxygenates can be processed through catalytic or in situ liquefaction combined with integrated carbon mineralization. This approach enhances hydrogen ­(H2) yields while simultaneously generating multiple valuable carbonbased products.[56] This coupling lowers energy demands and facilitates multi-product ­CO2 conversion pathways, including methanol and ethylene glycol, due to nickel and platinum catalytic effects, coupling oxygenate reforming with carbon mineralization.[57]

With the modification of the reaction, ­CO2 can also be reduced and photocatalyzed to the desired carbon products. Yoshino et  al. introduced heterogeneous photocatalysts targeting artificial photosynthesis for the reduction of ­CO2 using water as an electron donor [Fig. 4(a)].[58] With water serving as a Lewis base, it is possible to achieve ΔG > 0 in the ­CO2 reduction process of artificial photosynthesis. Single particulate photocatalysts with wide band gaps (e.g., Ag cocatalyst) can enhance the photocatalytic ­CO2 reduction process to achieve an efficient ­CO2 conversion process with water as an electron donor, leading to the synthesis selectivity of CO and ­H2. When combined with layered chalcogenide structure photocatalysts ­BaLa4Ti4O15, 38%, 60%, and 76% CO selectivity are achieved

in the loading methods of impregnation, ­H2 reduction, and liquid-phase reduction, respectively. Z-scheme ­CO2 reduction is fabricated as an artificial photocatalytic system to mimic the electron transfer pathway in natural photosynthesis. Consisting of ­CuGaS2 as reduced photocatalyst, ­TiO2 as photocatalyst for ­O2 release, and reduced graphene oxide (rGO) as solid-state electron mediator, this photocatalyzed Z-scheme system can be used for water splitting and ­CO2 reduction to form CO products.[59] Other systems, such as Co-complex electron mediators and non-electron mediators, are also capable of realizing the Z-scheme, but further optimization of CO selectivity is still needed. Multiple cyanobacteria/chloroplastbased photocatalytic processes and photocatalysts have also been widely explored. Wang et al. introduce a hybrid bioticabiotic system by directly using bacteria for ­CO2 fixing [Fig. 4(b and c)], where ­CH3COO− can be selectively produced and oxygen released using only sunlight, ­CO2, and ­H2O through a relatively inexpensive and readily available preparation method in combination with ­CO2-fixing acetic acid-producing bacteria (S. ovata), and achieve a solar-to-acetate conversion efficiency of 0.7% at 298 K, 1 atm.[60] Nosrati et al. synthesized hierarchical nanostructured graphene oxide (GO)-TiO2-Ag2O and GO-TiO2-Ag2O-Arginine (Arg) materials, which exhibited ­CO2 capture and selective synthesis of methanol [Fig. 4(d and e)]. Overall, based on the methods of carbon capture from natural cyanobacteria/chloroplasts, several modifications have been developed, such as increasing the efficiency of carbon fixation, optimizing product selectivity, or directly changing the product species. In future, the direction of improvement can focus on enhancing the efficiency of light energy utilization, optimizing the carbon fixation pathway, enhancing environmental adaptability, and expanding product diversity. At the same time, multidisciplinary crossover and dynamic regulation techniques could be applied to achieve a smarter and more efficient artificial carbon capture system.

Hybrid natural–synthetic materials The quest for efficient and sustainable ­CO2 capture technologies has led to the exploration of innovative material classes that combine the resilience and functionality of synthetic compounds with the environmental harmony of biological materials. As the material existing in nature can be advantageous in structural stability and ­CO2-philic due to reactive functional groups, an enhancement of ­CO2 capture efficiency can be achieved through the synthesis of material by learning from nature to engineer the configuration.[62] Hybrid bio-synthetic materials represent a pioneering category in ­CO2 capture technology, where the synergistic integration of naturally existing material arrangement and biomimetic

features opens new avenues for performance enhancement and application versatility. Nature has long optimized hierarchical porosity to facilitate efficient gas exchange, particularly in plants, where multiscale porous architectures facilitate nutrient and gas uptake. Ranging from macrospores with pores larger than 50 µm to mesopores with pore sizes between 2 and 50 µm, and to nanoscale pores in cell walls within a diameter of 2 µm, the hierarchical pores have evolved in plants to adapt to the surrounding nutrient and gas environments.[63] The development of pore structure, such as the vascular system in xylem and phloem, and the stomatal complex in plant tissue, balances gas exchange, enables selective transport of water and micronutrients, due to the pressure difference and concentration gradient, leading to efficient kinetics.[64,65] These naturally evolved structures serve as a template for designing advanced porous materials for gas and fluid separation and diffusion.[63,66] Inspired by this biological efficiency, MOFs have been developed with tunable pore structures that emulate the multilevel porosity found in plants. By mimicking these hierarchical features, MOFs can enhance ­CO2 accessibility, diffusion kinetics, and selectivity, offering a nature-informed pathway to highperformance adsorbents.[67] Recent advances in MOF research have demonstrated that strategic synthetic modifications and bioinspired design can remarkably enhance material porosity, catalytic performance, and gas adsorption capabilities. arranged mesopores with tunable dimensions ranging from 1.5 to 18 nm, controlling crystal defect formation for specific gas molecule diameters [Fig. 5(a)].[68] In addition, drawing inspiration from natural metalloporphyrins, researchers have engineered porous porphyrinic frameworks through a two-step synthesis that integrates functional polyoxometalates, leading to finely tuned pore structures and enhanced catalytic properties through the designed metalloporphyrins while mitigating issues like self-oxidation.[69] In addition to the structural inspiration, learning reaction mechanisms from nature can also provide elevated adsorption efficiency. By mimicking the active site of α-carbonic anhydrase, modifications in Zn benzotriazolate MOFs via mild postsynthetic ligand exchange and thermal activation have successfully introduced nucleophilic Zn-OH sites, thereby facilitating efficient trace ­CO2 adsorption capacity to 2.2 mmol ­g−1 at low partial pressures of 0.4 ­mbar[70] [Fig. 5(a)]. Together, these advancements underscore the potential of combining controlled defect engineering, bioinspiration, and postsynthetic modifications to tailor MOF functionalities for diverse applications ranging from heterogeneous catalysis to environmental remediation. Mimicking biological ­CO2 capture in tissues and lungs of organisms, the carbonic anhydrase (CA) is widely explored in materials for hydrating ­CO2 to bicarbonate at metal sites.[71] This bioinspired mechanism has been reported to involve a modification of genetic expressions and hydrogen bonding structures to enhance the thermal tolerance and absorption efficiency.[71–73] Further structural improvement demonstrated the performance of CA under high mechanical press conditions. Patel et al. first demonstrated that azo-linked covalent organic polymers (azo-COPs) could selectively reject ­N2, leading to a dramatic increase in ­CO2/N2 selectivity with temperature, which marked a significant innovation for post-combustion ­CO2 capture.[75] Building on this concept, a mixed matrix membrane (MMM) was synthesized by integrating Pebax-1657, a rubbery copolymer with high gas permeability and selectivity, with Co-2,6-bis(2-benzimidazolyl)pyridine (CoBBP), a biomimetic enzyme mimicking the active site of CA.[74] This MMM demonstrated exceptional thermal, mechanical, and aging stability while achieving a ­CO2 permeability of 675.5 Barrer and a ­CO2/N2 selectivity of 62%. Expanding upon this, Wang et al. synthesized another MMM by anchoring CoBBP on porous organic polymers (CoBBP@POP-1), featuring ­CO2-philic and ­N2-phobic properties due to the abundance of phenolic –OH and azo bonds.[75,76] Consequently, the ­CO2 permeability and ­CO2/N2 selectivity significantly exceeded pristine Pebax membrane and prior benchmarks as depicted in Fig. 5(c–e). While membrane and hierarchically porous systems learned from nature have advanced the physical design of ­CO2 capture systems, recent developments point to new classes of hybrid systems that draw inspiration not only from natural structures but also from biochemical mechanisms at the molecular level. These systems integrate bio-derived components with biomimetic catalytic or structural motifs, creating

multifunctional platforms for carbon fixation and capture. For example, enzyme-inspired inorganic complexes such as tetranuclear metal clusters and cryptand-based catalysts emulate the active sites of carbonic anhydrase and Rubisco, enabling selective and efficient ­CO2 binding through well-orchestrated reaction pathways.[77] Such molecular mimicry, informed by ab initio simulations, pushes the frontier of catalytic ­CO2 fixation toward cost-effective and scalable solutions. Complementing this, artificial nacre systems, replicated through layer-by-layer deposition or bulk assembly, combine crystalline ­CaCO3 platelets and polymeric interlayers to form organic-inorganic composites with high mechanical integrity and surface adaptability, closely mimicking the biological mineralization process.[78,79] Figure  6(a and b) show a bottom-up assembly process for this bulk artificial nacre and the fractured layered microstructure. Equipping the material with structural toughness, these nacre-like architectures also provide lamellar arrangement and interfacial chemistries that provide reactive and diffusion-friendly environments that can be tailored for predesigned matrix-directed ­CO2 mineralization and conversion, as shown in Fig. 6(c).[80] Together, these examples represent a class of hybrid systems that go beyond passive adsorption, offering integrated functionality, chemical activity, and mechanical robustness derived from both naturally abundant materials and nature-inspired pathways. Characterization and performance analysis Nature-learned ­CO2 removal materials are of great scientific interest as they consist of solid materials that directly capture, mineralize, or reduce ­CO2 with the specific reactive sites developed for adsorption and substrate that is composed of modified microbe and amine adsorbents for ­CO2 conversion and adsorption.[10,81–83] With the unique properties in raw material or chemical state, the characterization techniques are primarily associated with their physical and chemical natures, such as diameter, morphology, and atomic or molecular structures.[84] In materials science research, newly developed ­CO2 capture materials will need to undergo rigorous and comprehensive characterization to validate their potential strengths and weaknesses and to elucidate the specific mechanisms involved in the capture process. For adsorbents with predictable crystal structures, the raw and adsorbed material crystal structure is tested using powder X-ray diffraction (XRD). This method aims to verify the material’s crystallinity and determine its lattice parameters, which can also be cross-validated with theoretical calculations. Specifically, ­CO2 sorption in the naturally derived activated carbon complexed with alkali metals can be examined by the difference in crystallinity intensity and phase identification between metal carbonate

To determine the chemical reaction occurred during the ­CO2 adsorption, the chemical state of key functional groups involved in the adsorbent can be identified by researchers using nuclear magnetic resonance (NMR), Raman spectroscopy, and X-ray photoelectron spectroscopy (XPS) to conduct in situ and ex situ change of carbon bonding related to ­CO2 and the adsorbent.[88–90] In recent studies, techniques such as solidstate NMR have become increasingly popular due to their

fast magic-angle spinning and cross-polarization.[91] It has dramatically improved the sensitivity of nuclei and resolution of weakly responding sites to provide detailed insights into specific chemical groups and molecular configuration before and after ­CO2 reactions, even in disordered or non-crystalline materials. Although the mechanistic investigation of ­CO2 absorption, adsorption, fixation, conversion, and reduction can be diverse in characterization methods, the performance analysis for ­CO2 removal persistence and kinetics can be uniform. Temperature Swing Adsorption (TSA) and Pressure Swing Adsorption (PSA) are commonly used to reflect the time needed to desorb ­CO2 and regenerate the initial adsorbent or solvent.[92,93] During the swing process, the performance can reveal thermal stability and desorption behavior since it probes how strongly ­CO2 is chemisorbed and how external heat affects gas regeneration, as well as the affinity and selectivity by evaluating how ­CO2 uptake

Toward the application of ­CO2 capture in industrial processes, water vapor in flue gas can adversely affect the adsorption efficiency and cyclability of materials by degrading the adsorbent and absorbent and promoting undesired reactions due to competitive adsorption of water, lack of hydrophobicity of solid materials to humidity, or

possible pore blocking.[97,98] Correspondingly, due to the ­CO2 concentration in the atmosphere being relatively low compared to other gases, the breakthrough experiments can simulate the realistic air and post-combustion conditions for the implication of the real-time ­CO2 uptake kinetics, selectivity, and mass transfer behavior under dynamic flow conditions by tracking time when the adsorbent or absorbent becomes saturated and ­CO2 starts “breaking through.”[99,100] Through these comprehensive characterization and performance tests, experimental findings can be generated and imply the compelling scientific merit of the sorption process and scalability potential, thereby advancing the field of ­CO2 removal.

## Early Career Materials Researcher Prospective

MRS COMMUNICATIONS · VOLUME 15 · ISSUE 4 · www.mrs.org/mrc         633

Conclusion The nature-inspired materials, such as cellulose, lignin, starch, biochar, and chitosan, show potential for effective carbon capture due to their abundance and economic and environmental advantages. Additionally, indirectly inspired processes and materials from nature exhibit novel chemical features and possibilities, such as MOFs and microalgae. However, compared with mature industrial carbon capture methodologies, these innovative nature-inspired materials typically do not display significantly superior thermodynamic or kinetic properties, thus facing the problem of low efficiency or low recyclability, which indicates the high cost. Therefore, specific enhancements are necessary to modify these materials and unlock their full potential. Currently, extensive research is being conducted on the enhancement and modification through hybridizing nature-inspired materials, to achieve more efficient and cost-effective carbon capture. For upscaling the directly, indirectly, and hybrid inspired material from nature, it is necessary to understand the natural pathway related to carbon fluxes and fundamentals of the material that comprises the adsorbent and absorbent. In order to leverage the nature for gigaton ­CO2 capture, focus needs to be placed on the inherent properties of naturally abundant materials, which can facilitate large-scale capacity and efficient mass transfer, further enhancing the potential of nature-inspired carbon capture, utilization, and storage.
